claims.text: The proposed intervention is a single gradient-quenching protocol consisting of an ultrafast initial quench followed by a controlled, slower cooling tail.
Gradient quenching will improve glass-forming ability relative to a standard ultrarapid quench.
Gradient quenching will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state relative to a standard ultrarapid quench.
Rapid cooling during melt-spinning can produce an amorphous phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy.
The ultrafast initial cooling stage prevents crystal nucleation.
A moderated cooling tail permits limited atomic rearrangement in the amorphous alloy.
The moderated cooling tail reduces free volume and relieves internal stresses.
Gradient quenching enhances short-range order relative to standard ultrarapid quenching.
A more relaxed amorphous structure with reduced free volume resists crystallization during subsequent heating.
Structural relaxation produced by the cooling tail increases the crystallization onset temperature.
Gradient-quenched specimens will have a larger critical casting diameter than specimens subjected to a standard ultrarapid quench.
Gradient-quenched specimens will have a higher DSC crystallization onset temperature than specimens subjected to a standard ultrarapid quench.
Phosphorus produces significant local atomic-size mismatch and topological complexity in the relevant alloys.
Sufficient phosphorus facilitates amorphization in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
The benefit of the moderated cooling tail will be diminished in alloys with inherently low free volume or severely restricted atomic mobility.
Conventionally ultrarapid-quenched phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys have high free volume and relatively low thermal stability.
The amorphous phase is metastable, forms under kinetic control, and crystallizes when sufficient thermal activation is supplied.
DSC can identify the crystallization onset temperature of an amorphous high-entropy alloy.
XRD and high-resolution TEM can confirm amorphous structure and reveal short-range-order signatures.
XRD or high-resolution TEM can directly assess free-volume differences between the two quenching conditions.
